name: witr
why: Explains why a process is running by tracing its causes; a neat look at process ancestry, though a niche small tool.

brief.what_it_is: witr is a command-line tool (with an interactive terminal dashboard) that explains why a process, port, container, or file is running by tracing it back to the chain of things that started it. You give it a process name, PID, port, file path, or container name, and it prints a narrative of the ancestry chain (for example systemd → pm2 → node), the source that supervises it, the working directory, sockets, and warnings. Output can be human-readable text, a short or tree view, or JSON for scripts. It is distributed as a single static binary for Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, and Windows.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says existing tools like ps, top, lsof, ss, systemctl, and docker ps show what is running but leave the user to infer why by correlating output across tools. witr's stated aim is to make that causality explicit in one readable answer.
brief.how_it_works: witr maps a target (name, port, file, container, or PID) to a PID, then builds a causal ancestry chain for that PID and picks one primary source, such as a systemd unit, launchd job, container, pm2, cron, SSH session, or tmux session. Per the README it reads /proc on Linux, uses ps, lsof, sysctl and pgrep on macOS, uses procstat, ps and lsof on FreeBSD, and calls Win32 APIs directly on Windows. If the original parent has exited, the chain marks the break rather than guessing. Exit codes (0 clean, 1 warnings, 2 not found, 3 permission denied, 4 invalid input, 5 internal error, 6 cause unknown) let scripts act on the result.

brief.install_notes: No accounts or runtimes are required for the binary. Options are the install script, Homebrew, MacPorts, Conda/mamba/pixi, AUR, winget, Chocolatey, Scoop, npm, FreeBSD pkg or ports, apt on recent Debian/Ubuntu, deb/rpm/apk release packages, go install, Nix flake, and pixi exec. The install script verifies a SHA256 checksum optionally. On Windows the PowerShell script adds the bin directory to the user PATH. Shell completions are enabled with eval "$(witr completion bash)" (or zsh) or witr completion fish. Container lookups need the relevant runtime CLI (docker, podman, nerdctl, crictl, incus, lxc, jls) on PATH. Full visibility often needs sudo on Linux/FreeBSD/macOS, or an Administrator terminal on Windows.
brief.standout: It treats every question (port, service, container, file) as a question about a PID and then explains the causal chain, rather than just listing state. It also has an explicit design for AI coding agents: a stable JSON contract, documented exit codes, and a suggested AGENTS.md snippet. A browser-based simulated Linux box lets people try it without installing.
brief.status: unknown. The README shows a Latest Release badge and lists many packagers (Debian, Homebrew, AUR, Winget, Conda, FreeBSD ports), and it refers to Ubuntu 26.04 and a Hacker News discussion, which suggests active use. However, no release date, last commit date, or maintenance note appears in the fetched README, so I cannot confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: The README does not state a license, so reuse terms are unknown. Platform support differs: Windows lacks tmux/screen detection, schedule detection, file locks, process actions, and some other features; macOS lacks capability warnings, and SIP blocks some process details even with sudo; FreeBSD lacks restart counts and schedule detection. Process actions (kill, pause, renice) are Unix only. Some details require sudo or an Administrator terminal. Without a terminal the TUI will not open, and output-mode flags without a target exit with code 4. The README calls the source selection best-effort. The brew caveats field was empty.
quotes: Trace any process, port, container, or file back to the exact chain that started it — one command, machine-readable JSON, or an interactive TUI.
witr treats everything as a process question.

entry.title: witr
entry.tldr: witr answers "why is this running?" for a process, port, container or file by tracing it back through the chain of parents that started it.
entry.deeper_look:
witr takes a process name, PID, port, file path or container name and prints a short narrative of where it came from. The output is an ancestry chain such as systemd → pm2 → node, plus the thing that supervises it, the working directory, open sockets and any warnings. It can print plain text, a short or tree view, or JSON, and there is an interactive terminal dashboard.

The README's complaint is that ps, top, lsof, ss, systemctl and docker ps each show what is running, but you have to correlate their output yourself to work out why. witr tries to give that causality in one answer.

The idea underneath is in the project's own words: "witr treats everything as a process question." A port, a locked file and a container are each mapped to a PID, and then the parent chain is walked. It picks one primary source, such as a systemd unit, launchd job, container, pm2, cron, SSH session or tmux session. If the original parent has exited, the chain marks the break instead of guessing. That makes it a handy way to learn how process ancestry, supervisors and orphaned children actually work on your machine.

It reads /proc on Linux and uses ps, lsof and similar tools on macOS and FreeBSD. On Windows it calls Win32 APIs directly. Exit codes distinguish clean runs, warnings, not found, permission denied and cause unknown, so scripts can act on the result.
entry.install:
brew install witr
# Also available via an install script, MacPorts, apt on recent Debian/Ubuntu, AUR, winget, Scoop, npm, go install, Nix and others.
# Full visibility often needs sudo (Administrator terminal on Windows). Container lookups need the relevant runtime CLI (docker, podman, etc.) on PATH.

entry.whats_unique: It turns every question about a port, file or container into a question about a PID, then explains the causal chain instead of listing state. It also ships a stable JSON contract and documented exit codes aimed at scripts and AI coding agents.
entry.caveats: Source selection is described as best-effort, some details need sudo, and platform support varies: Windows lacks tmux/screen and schedule detection, and macOS SIP hides some process details even with sudo.
